--- gd-head-tags: - >- ``{=html} open-graph: title: >- [Graph.dominance_frontiers()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | EdgeCase description: >- Find the dominance frontier of every node reachable from a start node. twitter-card: title: >- [Graph.dominance_frontiers()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | EdgeCase description: >- Find the dominance frontier of every node reachable from a start node. title: >- [Graph.dominance_frontiers()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 bread-crumbs: false toc-depth: 3 description-meta: >- Find the dominance frontier of every node reachable from a start node. page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Find the dominance frontier of every node reachable from a start node. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L74708-L74842){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-function} ```pythonsignature Graph.dominance_frontiers(source) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Dominance frontiers](../assets/graphs/dominance-frontiers.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="The same if/else control-flow graph from entry. The branches then and else are outlined: each dominates only itself, and its edge into merge (accent) leaves its region, so merge, filled in accent, is the dominance frontier of both. The card lists every node's frontier: merge for then and else, and empty for the others." width="100%"} The dominance frontier of a node `d` is the set of nodes where `d`'s dominance ends: the nodes `v` that `d` does not strictly dominate, but that have a predecessor dominated by `d` (see `immediate_dominators()`). They are the merge points where paths from inside and outside `d`'s region meet. Compilers use them to place phi functions when building static single assignment form; in other networks they mark where the influence of an unavoidable node stops being exclusive. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [source]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Union[int, str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The start (entry) node, as an ID or label. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [dict[int, set[int]]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : For every node ID reachable from `source`, the set of node IDs in its frontier. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the graph is undirected or `source` does not exist. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} Following Cooper, Harvey and Kennedy (2001), as in NetworkX: for every join node `v` (two or more predecessors), each reachable predecessor walks up the dominator tree until reaching `v`'s immediate dominator, adding `v` to the frontier of every node passed. The start node has no immediate dominator, so an edge back into it makes it a join whose walk climbs up to and including the start: the start is then in its own frontier. The cost is proportional to the total size of the frontiers after computing the dominators. ## See Also {.doc-see-also} [](`~immediate_dominators`) : The last node that every path to a node passes. ## Examples {.doc-examples} In an if/else, the frontier of each branch is the node where the branches rejoin: ::: {#b9959fd7 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ec.Graph.from_edges( [("entry", "if"), ("if", "then"), ("if", "else"), ("then", "merge"), ("else", "merge"), ("merge", "exit")], directed=True, ) label = graph.get_label_from_id { label(n): [label(m) for m in frontier] for n, frontier in graph.dominance_frontiers("entry").items() } ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` {'entry': [], 'if': [], 'then': ['merge'], 'else': ['merge'], 'merge': [], 'exit': []} ``` ::: ::: ### Where a branch rejoins the plan `project()` is the plan for opening a made-up café, with an arrow from each task to every task that can't start until it's done. A task's dominance frontier holds the tasks where its part of the plan meets work that doesn't go through it. The design's frontier is the training and the health inspection, which also wait on the hiring and the suppliers: ::: {#4dd6127d .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} cafe = ec.project() label = cafe.get_label_from_id frontiers = cafe.dominance_frontiers("Start") { label(n): sorted(label(m) for m in frontiers[n]) for n in [cafe.get_id_from_label(t) for t in ["Design", "Plan menu"]] } ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` {'Design': ['Health inspection', 'Training'], 'Plan menu': ['Health inspection', 'Soft opening']} ``` ::: ::: ::: {#9e9415e3 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} cafe.plot( layout="pos", highlight={"accent": "Design", "soft": list(frontiers[cafe.get_id_from_label("Design")])}, label_by="label", height=360, ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ### Where paths merge in a function `control_flow()` is the control flow graph of a short function, with a node for each basic block of code and an edge for each possible jump. The frontier of `negate` is `add`, where the paths with and without `x = -x` meet again: the place a compiler in SSA form puts a φ-function for `x`. The two ways out of the loop meet at `empty test`, and the frontier of `loop` is `loop` itself, the sign of a loop header: ::: {#ec9f1b86 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} cfg = ec.control_flow() label = cfg.get_label_from_id frontiers = cfg.dominance_frontiers("entry") { b: sorted(label(m) for m in frontiers[cfg.get_id_from_label(b)]) for b in ["negate", "break", "loop"] } ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` {'negate': ['add'], 'break': ['empty test'], 'loop': ['loop']} ``` ::: ::: `negate` is drawn in full and its frontier pale: ::: {#55f2f6cd .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} negate = cfg.get_id_from_label("negate") cfg.plot( layout="pos", highlight={"accent": {negate}, "soft": frontiers[negate]}, label_by="label", edge_label_by="branch", ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: [Directed acyclic graphs](../user-guide/dags.qmd#dominators) finds the dominator tree of a loop's control flow.
